strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting task-specific real abnormal footage. Using class-conditioned synthetic videos as replacement supervision, rather than only as augmentation, is a useful direction for computer vision.

The reported results are promising: 98.2% frame-level AUC on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime. With the same synthetic training data, DARM improves over the UR-DMU backbone by 2.2 and 2.3 points, respectively, providing evidence that the detector adaptation contributes beyond video generation.

The ShanghaiTech component ablations and synthetic-data scaling experiment provide useful supporting evidence. The supplement supplies generation settings, training hyperparameters, computational costs, and a concrete generation failure case. The discussion appropriately acknowledges difficulties with subtle, long-duration anomalies.
weaknesses: The comparison protocols do not adequately support the strongest claims. Section 4.1 uses the revised weakly supervised ShanghaiTech test split, but Table 4 does not establish that the quoted UVAD results use this same split or were reevaluated on it. Moreover, PA-VAD receives target anomaly class names and substantial pretrained generative and semantic knowledge, so absence of real abnormal training videos alone does not make its comparison with normal-only UVAD 'fully fair.' The paper should distinguish these supervision resources and provide matched-protocol comparisons.

The proposed explanation for DARM is insufficiently validated. Table 1 reports only average real/pseudo feature norms, without distributions, uncertainty, or evidence that high-norm instances dominate MIL selection. Equations (10)–(11) explicitly normalize features and memories before assignment, so the claimed relationship between raw magnitude and slot monopolization requires further justification. Alignment of normal streams also does not establish alignment of abnormal streams. Before/after norm statistics, slot usage, selected-instance analysis, and a simple feature-normalization baseline would help distinguish magnitude correction from generic regularization.

Key experimental controls are missing. Every row of Table 5 uses initial-image selection, leaving its contribution untested against random or scene-matched selection. There is no matched comparison with the closest pseudo-anomaly generation approaches discussed in Section 2.2, nor a comparison of usage weighting against an unweighted prototype-center penalty. Consequently, the evidence does not clearly isolate the value of the proposed design beyond combining established generation, prompting, domain-adversarial learning, and memory components.

Reproduction is impeded by ambiguous or inconsistent implementation details. The stated Qwen3 30B-A3B checkpoint is not identified as a vision-capable model despite receiving images. The supplement reports an RTX 6000 Ada with 100 GB memory and approximately 95,776 MiB usage, inconsistent with that GPU's standard 48 GB capacity. Pseudo-normal generation prompts, the detector feature-extractor configuration, training duration and checkpoint-selection procedure, assignment temperature, and gradient handling through the usage-weighted centers are also insufficiently specified. These details affect both reproducibility and interpretation of the method.

The empirical reliability and deployment claims exceed the available evidence. Results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates despite stochastic generation and training; this particularly matters for the 0.6-point ShanghaiTech advantage. Component and data-volume ablations are confined to ShanghaiTech, while UCF-Crime lacks per-class results that could reveal failures on subtle anomalies. No held-out anomaly-category or scene-transfer experiment supports broader robustness claims. Although the reported gains justify continued investigation, the protocol, mechanism, and reproducibility concerns currently outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful practical problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal footage. Replacing abnormal training videos with class-conditioned synthetic clips is a useful direction, even without achieving the best fully supervised results.

The reported results are promising: 98.2% frame-level AUC on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime. Adding DARM to the same synthetic-data UR-DMU baseline improves AUC by 2.2 and 2.3 points, respectively, providing evidence that the detector modifications are useful.

The ShanghaiTech component and data-volume ablations provide useful supporting evidence. Prompt refinement improves both detection and several generation metrics, while the memory update contributes substantially to detection performance.

The supplement provides generation settings, training coefficients, computational costs, and unsuccessful synthesis examples. The discussion of difficulties with subtle, long-duration anomalies appropriately acknowledges an important limitation.
weaknesses: The headline UVAD comparison is not established as protocol-matched. Section 4.1 explicitly evaluates ShanghaiTech using the revised weakly supervised split, whereas Table 4 lists UVAD results without establishing that they were rerun on that split with the same normal training data. Moreover, PA-VAD uses known abnormal-category names and pretrained generative/semantic models, which supply additional information beyond normal-only learning. Calling the comparison 'fully fair' merely because neither approach trains on task-specific real abnormal videos overlooks these differences.

The explanation for DARM remains insufficiently supported. Table 1 reports only an average feature-norm difference, 20.52 versus 23.03; it does not demonstrate that high-norm synthetic instances monopolize MIL selection or that DARM corrects this behavior. Alignment of real and synthetic normal features does not itself establish alignment of abnormal features. Before/after norm distributions, slot utilization, and MIL-selection statistics are needed to substantiate the proposed mechanism.

Equation (13) encourages underused prototypes to approach their responsibility-weighted centers, but does not explicitly enforce balanced usage or distinct abnormal modes. Prototype collapse is compatible with this objective. The empirical gains are valuable, but comparisons against feature normalization, ordinary prototype-center regularization, and explicit usage balancing would clarify what the proposed weighting contributes.

The experimental controls do not adequately isolate the contribution beyond combining existing components. Every row of Table 5 uses initial-image selection, so its advantage over random or scene-balanced seeds is untested. The closest pseudo-anomaly approaches discussed in related work are absent from the quantitative comparisons. A matched comparison using the same backbone and normal data would better establish the value of CA-PAG.

Important reproduction details are missing or inconsistent. The stated Qwen3-30B-A3B model is a text model, leaving the image-conditioned refinement implementation unclear. The supplement reports an 'RTX 6000 Ada 100 GB' GPU, inconsistent with that model's standard 48 GB capacity. Pseudo-normal generation, the exact detector feature-extraction configuration, training duration, and checkpoint-selection protocol also need clearer specification. These issues affect reconstruction of the pipeline and interpretation of its cost.

The evidence does not establish the stability or breadth of the claimed gains. There are no repeated-run uncertainties, component ablations are confined to ShanghaiTech, and the 0.6-point advantage over its strongest listed real-abnormal baseline lacks a controlled replication. Generation metrics omit the real reference subset and sampling details, so their use of real abnormal data for evaluation versus development is unclear. These gaps matter more than the acknowledged UCF-Crime performance limitation and leave the overall case for acceptance unconvincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal footage. Replacing abnormal training videos with class-conditioned synthetic clips is a useful contribution, even without surpassing fully supervised alternatives.

The strongest evidence is the controlled comparison against UR-DMU trained on the same synthetic data: DARM improves AUC from 96.0% to 98.2% on ShanghaiTech and from 80.2% to 82.5% on UCF-Crime. These consistent gains support the utility of the proposed detector modifications.

The ShanghaiTech component ablations and synthetic-data scaling study provide useful evidence. Prompt refinement improves the unregularized detector, usage-aware updates contribute substantially, and combining the components achieves the best reported result.

The manuscript clearly attributes the underlying models and detector backbone, provides additional generation and training settings, and acknowledges synthesis failures and difficulties with long-duration anomalies. The supplementary failure examples help delimit the approach’s capabilities.
weaknesses: The fairness of the headline UVAD comparisons is not established. PA-VAD uses the revised weakly supervised ShanghaiTech evaluation split, but Table 4 does not establish that the quoted UVAD results use that same test set. Moreover, PA-VAD receives anticipated anomaly class names and substantial pretrained semantic knowledge, so the absence of real abnormal training footage alone does not make the comparison 'fully fair.' Matched-split results and explicit accounting of supervision are needed.

The experimental controls do not sufficiently isolate the contribution beyond applying powerful pretrained generators. Table 5 always enables initial-image selection, leaving its benefit untested. There is no matched comparison with random seed-image selection, an existing pseudo-anomaly method, or a direct vision-language baseline using the same class metadata. Component ablations are confined to ShanghaiTech despite the different challenges on UCF-Crime.

The explanation that DARM corrects magnitude-driven MIL bias is stronger than the evidence. Table 1 reports only average feature norms, without distributions, top-k selection statistics, memory occupancy, or measurements showing that DARM actually removes the proposed bias. Aligning normal streams does not by itself establish alignment of abnormal streams, and the memory assignments already use cosine similarity. A feature-normalization baseline and direct measurements would help distinguish the claimed mechanism from generic regularization.

Important reproduction details remain ambiguous despite the supplement. The image-conditioned prompt refiner is identified as Qwen3 30B-A3B, which is not identified as a vision-language checkpoint; the exact multimodal model or image interface needs clarification. The reported 'RTX 6000 Ada 100 GB' hardware also conflicts with that model’s standard memory specification. Pseudo-normal generation, checkpoint selection, and the validation protocol are insufficiently described, making it difficult to verify both the implementation and the abnormal-free model-selection claim.

All reported results are single values without variability across generation or training seeds. This particularly limits confidence in the 0.6-point ShanghaiTech advantage over the strongest listed real-abnormal baseline. The practical promise and consistent backbone improvements make the decision close, but the unresolved evaluation comparability and missing controls leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful practical problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal footage. Generating scene-conditioned anomalies from normal training images and class names is a useful direction with potential deployment value.

The strongest evidence is the controlled comparison within PA-VAD: adding DARM to the same UR-DMU pipeline improves AUC from 96.0 to 98.2 on ShanghaiTech, 80.2 to 82.5 on UCF-Crime, and 92.5 to 95.1 on XD-Violence (Table 4). These consistent improvements support the usefulness of the regularization.

The ShanghaiTech ablations examine image selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, memory updates, and synthetic-data quantity. In particular, class-relevant seed selection provides a substantial improvement, and Table 6 demonstrates useful performance with relatively few generated clips.

The manuscript attributes its inherited components, acknowledges the additional pretrained knowledge relative to UVAD, and discusses generation failures and difficulty with context-heavy anomalies. The supplementary generation settings, training hyperparameters, and computational costs are helpful.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons do not adequately control feature representations or evaluation protocols. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, whereas key baselines use I3D, C3D, or other representations, with results quoted from prior papers. Matched-backbone real-only, pseudo-only, and normal-only comparisons are needed to separate generation benefits from stronger pretrained features. ShanghaiTech additionally uses the revised weakly supervised split without establishing that the quoted UVAD results use the same test set. These issues materially weaken the superiority claims.

The proposed magnitude-bias mechanism is only partially established. Table 5b gives one real-abnormal norm per dataset alongside three differently trained pseudo-abnormal conditions; real and pseudo norms should be measured within each corresponding model. Mean norms alone do not establish that magnitude drives MIL selection or memory monopolization. Comparisons with simple feature normalization, norm regularization, and an unweighted memory-center loss, together with slot-usage and Top-k diagnostics, would distinguish the proposed mechanism from generic regularization.

Equation (14) pulls memories toward responsibility-weighted centers but does not directly enforce balanced assignments or smaller feature norms. Its behavior depends on whether gradients flow through assignments, usage weights, and centers, which is unspecified. Because these quantities depend on the memories and embeddings, the stated interpretation as a targeted update of underused slots is not sufficient to characterize the actual optimization.

Important implementation details are inconsistent or missing. Section 4.1 calls Qwen2.5-VL an auxiliary extractor for analysis, while Table 4 identifies it as the detector backbone. The named Qwen3 30B-A3B checkpoint is a text model rather than the stated vision-language model, requiring clarification of the actual image-conditioned refinement implementation. Pseudo-normal generation, feature extraction and temporal pooling, assignment temperature, and the validation/model-selection protocol are also insufficiently specified. In particular, the paper does not establish whether real abnormal validation examples influenced configuration selection.

The open-set experiments report aggregate AUC over seen and unseen classes, rather than isolating held-out anomaly performance. PA-VAD averages three random class splits while baselines are quoted from their papers, without establishing matched splits. No open-set DARM ablation supports the specific attribution of transfer gains to usage-aware updates. These results are encouraging but do not substantiate the stronger mechanistic generalization claims.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the central algorithmic addition needs stronger isolation: the framework combines established retrieval, prompting, diffusion generation, domain adversarial learning, and UR-DMU with a weighted prototype loss. Main results lack repeated-run uncertainty, despite small headline margins over selected baselines. The practical contribution has merit, but the comparison, mechanism, and reproducibility concerns collectively favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal training footage. Replacing such footage with scene-conditioned synthetic anomalies is a useful contribution direction under Algorithms/General.

The pipeline is coherent: CLIP selects scene-relevant normal images, prompt refinement conditions video generation, and DARM adapts an established detector to synthetic supervision. The manuscript appropriately attributes the underlying models and UR-DMU architecture.

The controlled comparisons within PA-VAD provide encouraging evidence. With the same Qwen2.5-VL features and synthetic data, DARM improves over UR-DMU from 96.0 to 98.2 AUC on ShanghaiTech, 80.2 to 82.5 on UCF-Crime, and 92.5 to 95.1 on XD-Violence. Table 5 also separates generation and regularization components.

The supplementary material reports generation settings, training hyperparameters, computational costs, and synthesis failures. The discussion of difficulty with long-duration, context-dependent anomalies is relevant and appropriately acknowledges a limitation.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons do not adequately control evaluation protocol and representation. ShanghaiTech uses the revised weakly supervised test split, while UVAD results are quoted from original papers without establishing that they use this same split. Table 4 also compares PA-VAD's Qwen2.5-VL features against I3D, C3D, and other representations. These comparisons cannot isolate the benefits of synthetic supervision or establish the claimed superiority over UVAD and real-abnormal training. Matched-feature, matched-split baselines are needed, including real-abnormal UR-DMU and an appropriate normal-only baseline.

The central magnitude-bias explanation is suggestive rather than established. Table 5b gives one real-abnormal norm alongside pseudo-abnormal norms from three differently trained models; it does not report real and pseudo distributions separately for every model at a clearly specified layer. Consequently, it cannot distinguish improved domain alignment from general feature rescaling. There are also no direct measurements of MIL selection concentration or memory-slot coverage, and no comparisons against simple feature normalization, norm regularization, or an unweighted prototype-center loss. These controls are important because magnitude correction and usage balancing constitute the main algorithmic justification.

The usage-aware loss does not itself establish balanced prototype coverage. Pulling underused slots toward their responsibility-weighted centers can move several slots toward similar regions, and the manuscript provides neither a diversity analysis nor a direct coverage measurement to exclude this outcome. The dependence of assignments, centers, and usage weights on trainable features also makes gradient handling consequential, but detach/update details are unspecified.

The open-set results do not substantiate the specific claim that DARM improves unseen-class generalization. Tables 8–9 report aggregate AUC on the full test set, combining seen and unseen classes, and contain no corresponding PA-VAD-without-DARM ablation. Prior results are quoted rather than evaluated on the same sampled class splits and features. Unseen-only or per-class results and matched ablations are needed to support the proposed anti-specialization mechanism.

Several reproducibility details remain unresolved despite the supplementary material. Section 4.1 describes Qwen2.5-VL as an auxiliary analysis/metrics extractor, whereas Table 4 identifies it as the detector backbone. The image-conditioned prompt refiner is identified as Qwen3 30B-A3B with a Qwen3 reference, leaving its visual interface/checkpoint unclear. Pseudo-normal generation, feature temporal sampling and pooling, training duration, and checkpoint selection are insufficiently specified. The validation protocol is particularly important because the work claims to avoid real abnormal training footage while selecting dataset-dependent settings.

Experimental uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Standard deviations are provided only for open-set class sampling, not the principal results or ablations, although synthetic generation introduces additional variation and some headline margins are below one AUC point. Generation-quality claims also overinterpret FVD/KVD as evidence of physical plausibility, and equal rounded KID values do not establish identical image statistics. Overall, the promising internal improvements support further investigation, but the comparative and mechanistic evidence is not yet strong enough for acceptance.

strengths: PA-VAD addresses an important practical problem: training video anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal footage. Combining scene-conditioned video synthesis with adaptation to synthetic supervision is a useful contribution, assessed here as Algorithms/General.

The results are promising across three datasets. Under the same pseudo-data and feature setting, adding DARM improves UR-DMU from 96.0 to 98.2 AUC on ShanghaiTech, 80.2 to 82.5 on UCF-Crime, and 92.5 to 95.1 on XD-Violence (Table 4). These consistent gains provide meaningful evidence beyond comparisons with published baselines.

The ShanghaiTech ablations substantiate several design choices: CLIP-based seed selection provides a substantial improvement, prompt refinement adds further benefit, and the memory-update regularizer contributes most of DARM's gain. The pseudo-data quantity study also helps characterize the method's data requirements.

The manuscript acknowledges unequal pretrained knowledge relative to UVAD, discusses failures on subtle and long-duration anomalies, and reports generation costs and several implementation hyperparameters. The open-set experiments provide encouraging additional evidence of transfer.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, whereas key published competitors use I3D, C3D, or other representations (Table 4). A real-abnormal UR-DMU baseline using the same Qwen features would clarify the effect of replacing real anomalies with generated ones. Moreover, ShanghaiTech uses a revised WVAD test split while UVAD results are quoted from original papers; identical evaluation splits are not established. These concerns weaken the claimed superiority over UVAD and real-abnormal training.

The central magnitude-bias explanation remains incompletely demonstrated. Table 5b gives one real-anomaly norm per dataset but pseudo-anomaly norms from three training configurations, leaving unclear whether real and pseudo features are compared within each corresponding learned space. Reduced norms could reflect general rescaling rather than improved alignment. Per-model real/pseudo distributions, memory-usage statistics, and controls using simple feature normalization or an unweighted memory-center loss would distinguish the proposed mechanism from generic regularization.

Reproducibility has material inconsistencies and omissions. Section 4.1 describes Qwen2.5-VL as auxiliary for analysis/metrics, but Table 4 identifies it as the detector backbone. The prompt-refinement model is named Qwen3 30B-A3B, a text model, without explaining its visual interface. The pseudo-normal generation procedure, feature pooling and frame sampling, assignment temperature, gradient handling through the memory targets, and training duration are insufficiently specified.

The open-set evidence does not establish the claimed DARM mechanism. Tables 8–9 evaluate the full test set, mixing seen and unseen anomalies, and compare new random splits with previously published results. Unseen-only performance on matched class splits and a DARM ablation under the open-set protocol are needed to support the assertion that usage-aware updates specifically improve unseen-class generalization.

The validation and model-selection protocol is unspecified despite dataset-dependent hyperparameters and a pseudo-data quantity sweep. The manuscript should explain how these choices were made without real abnormal validation supervision and distinguish that process from the retrospective real-anomaly analyses. Main results also lack repeated-run variability, making the small headline margins of 0.6–0.9 AUC points difficult to assess.

Overall, the consistent internal improvements make this a close decision, but unresolved comparison controls, reproducibility details, and evidence for the central mechanism currently favor borderline rejection.
